name: Freya Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and what you actually think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most days I start at seven at Greenhill Community Farm, which is run by a land trust, so it's owned by the community rather than one family. Mornings I do the sheep and the pigs, then I'm in the polytunnels or the veg beds, picking and packing for the box scheme. On Thursdays forty boxes go out in the van, and that's a mad scramble. I've been here two years, so Hannah, the farm manager, still checks my work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that people from the estate come up and volunteer, and kids see a pig for the first time. The hard bit is my contract runs one year at a time, because a chunk of my wage comes from a grant. Every March I'm waiting to hear if the money's renewed. My girlfriend Sam is a nurse at the district hospital, so we're okay, and we've got about four months of savings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I've asked a chatbot to help me write up the sheep notes, and once about a worming dose, though I checked it with the vet after. I'm not against it, I just don't trust it till I've seen it work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and that the real problems on farms were never going to be fixed by an app. I'd probably post something on the trust's page about how good food still needs people. With friends I'd laugh about all the money spent on hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my worries stay the same ones I have now. Every March I'm waiting to hear if the council grant that pays half my wage at Greenhill is renewed. If the council cuts it, my job goes back to part-time. Sam's wage keeps us steady, but I don't like being the one who might drop to three days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and I'd help Hannah write the grant renewal properly this time instead of leaving it to her. I'd keep the savings where they are, about four months, and try to add fifty a month. Maybe ask about a two-year contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with the usual knot in my stomach every spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the grant decides your hours. What happened last March?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last March the council letter came two weeks late, and Hannah had to tell three of us she didn't know if she could pay us in April. I spent those two weeks looking at jobs at the big dairy down the valley. Then the money came through and nobody talked about it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a job at the big dairy if the grant went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, because there are some jobs nearby, but I wouldn't like it. They milk five hundred cows in shifts and nobody knows the names of anything. I'd rather do three days at Greenhill and pick up shifts packing at the farm shop.

say: The real problems on farms were never going to be fixed by **an app**.
Good food still needs **people**, and I'd post that on the **trust's page**.
think: My worries stay the same: the **grant** runs out every **March**.
If the council cuts it, I drop to **three days** a week.
**Sam's nursing wage** keeps us steady, but I hate being the weak link.
do: Help Hannah write the **grant renewal** properly this year.
Add **fifty a month** to our four months of savings.
Ask the trust about a **two-year contract**.
feel: **Mostly fine**, with the usual **knot** in my stomach every spring.

Her partner's **steady nursing wage** is a quiet safety net she doesn't fully like relying on.

steps.text: Help Hannah write the council grant renewal before March
Add fifty a month to the joint savings with Sam

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI should do the boring bits so people can do the caring bits, on farms and in hospitals. I'd say it on the trust's page and at the landworkers' meeting. And I'd keep saying that the savings have to go to workers, not just owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a lot of it barely reaches me. The thinking stuff, like ordering seed and planning the box rounds, is Hannah's job and the volunteer coordinator's. My hands are in the soil and the pig pen, and robots spread there slowly. What worries me is the box scheme. If supermarkets get cleverer and cheaper with AI, our forty veg boxes at Greenhill could go down to twenty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI for my bits, like writing the sheep records and planning the tunnel planting, once I've seen Hannah use it without mistakes. I'd join the landworkers' union, which I've meant to do for a year. And I'd keep the savings ticking over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay. A bit unsettled, like when the weather forecast keeps changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Greenhill would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about Joy, the volunteer coordinator, because her job is mostly emails, rotas and the website. That's exactly what you said the AI takes. She's fifty-eight and she's been at Greenhill since the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see Hannah use it first. How long would that take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A season, probably. If Hannah's planting plan comes out right and the tomatoes don't all ripen in one week, I'd be in. I'm not the first to try things, but I'm not the last either.

say: AI should do the **boring bits** so people can do the **caring**.
The savings from AI have to reach **workers**, not just owners.
think: Most of the **thinking work** is Hannah's, so it barely reaches me.

do: Use AI for the **sheep records** and tunnel planting once proven.
Join the **landworkers' union** I've meant to join for a year.
Keep the **savings** ticking over at fifty a month.
feel: **Okay**, but a bit **unsettled**, like a forecast that keeps changing.
S1.quote: If supermarkets get cleverer and cheaper with AI, our forty veg boxes at Greenhill could go down to twenty-five.
fieldNote: She places herself on the **hands-on side**, with desk work landing on Hannah and Joy.

She'd adopt AI after **one season** of proof, which fits her steady style.

steps.text: Use a chatbot for sheep records after Hannah tests it
Join the landworkers' union this winter
Keep adding fifty a month to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a public emergency and it needs a public answer, like a wage for everyone and land kept for people. I'd be loud about it on the trust's page and at union meetings. I'd also say small community farms are worth protecting even if robots are cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, the first two years hit Hannah and Joy more than me, because the AI can plan and order better than them. Then the robots come around 2031, and a big farm with robots could sell veg boxes at half our price. Greenhill might survive as a place people visit, but I don't know if it pays wages. Sam's nursing job feels safer than mine, which is strange to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop looking at flats to buy, because a mortgage on two uncertain jobs is daft. I'd move the savings up to a hundred a month and keep three months untouched. I'd learn the AI tools properly now, for planning the tunnels, so I'm useful when the planning side changes. And I'd go to every meeting about a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels shaky. I can see the edge, but I've still got my hands on something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Sam's job feels safer. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's uncomfortable. I always thought I'd be the one bringing the outdoors stuff and Sam would bring the steady money, and that was fine. But if I lose Greenhill, I'm the one being carried, and I'd hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the volunteers from the estate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the estate volunteers that a robot can grow a carrot, but it can't teach a nine-year-old where carrots come from. Then I'd hope the council agrees with me when the budget comes round.

say: This is a **public emergency** and it needs a **public answer**.
Small **community farms** are worth protecting even when robots are cheaper.
think: The first two years hit **Hannah and Joy** more than me.

**Sam's nursing job** feels safer than mine, which unsettles me.
do: Stop looking at **flats to buy** with Sam for now.
Raise savings to **a hundred a month**, with three months untouched.

feel: **Shaky**, but still holding on to **something real**.
S2.quote: A robot can grow a carrot, but it can't teach a nine-year-old where carrots come from.
fieldNote: She sees the **gap clearly**: desk planning changes first, then robot farms undercut Greenhill.
Being **carried by Sam** would hurt her pride more than the money.
She'd put off **buying a flat**, a real change to her plans.
Her case for Greenhill rests on **teaching and community**, not price.

steps.text: Stop viewing flats to buy with Sam
Save a hundred a month and keep three months untouched
Learn AI planning tools for the Greenhill polytunnels

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough warning that nobody gets to act surprised. I'd push the trust to write a plan: what we'd automate, what we'd keep human, and how we'd keep paying staff. I'd talk about it at the union too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years feels a lot better than two. The thinking AI comes in 2031 and the robots around 2034, when I'm thirty-five. Greenhill moves slowly and can't afford robots early, so I think my job lasts longer than at the big dairy. The risk is still the box customers going elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a short course in livestock health at the college, two evenings a week, so I'm more than a pair of hands. I'd use AI tools for planning once I've seen them work for a season. And I'd keep the savings steady at four months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable. Not relaxed, but I'm not lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why livestock health, rather than something away from farms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like animals more than anything, and a sick ewe needs someone who notices her standing wrong. The vet told me farms will always need people who know the animals. I'm not sure that's true by 2034, but it's my best guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You trust Greenhill being slow. Is that a strength or a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, really. Being slow means Greenhill won't sack anyone for a robot in a hurry, but we might still pack boxes by hand at double the price. That's the honest trade.

say: With **five years** warning, nobody gets to act **surprised**.
The trust should write a **plan** for what stays **human**.
think: Five years feels much better, with robots around **2034**.
Greenhill is **slow and poor**, so my job likely outlasts the big dairy's.
The risk is still **box customers** going elsewhere.
do: Take a **livestock health course** two evenings a week.
Use **AI planning tools** after a season of proof.
S3.quote: Being slow means Greenhill won't sack anyone for a robot in a hurry, but we might still pack boxes by hand at double the price.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **build skills** rather than brace for a cut.
She sees Greenhill's **slowness** as both protection and a threat.
She picks **livestock health** because of what she loves, admitting it's a guess.

steps.text: Take a two-evening livestock health course at the college
Use AI planning tools after one tested season
Hold savings at four months of expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we shouldn't waste it arguing about whether it's real. I'd want the union and the trust to plan farm jobs for 2040 now. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking AI arrives and forty when the robots do. That's long enough to become properly good at something. I'd probably still be at Greenhill, or running a small place of my own with Sam. My worry is still the yearly grant more than the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Greenhill and do the part-time agriculture certificate over two years, so I could run a farm, not just work on one. I'd use AI for the planning side as it gets better. And I'd keep putting a bit by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels hopeful, with the usual March nerves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Sam really run a small place of your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about it on long walks. Sam wants to keep nursing, and I'd do the land, maybe goats and a small veg plot. It's a dream, but ten years makes dreams feel less silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the ten-year picture change how you feel about the grant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. If I've got a proper certificate, I'm less stuck waiting for the council letter every March. That would be the real win for me, more than anything about robots.

The union and trust should plan **farm jobs for 2040** now.
think: At **forty**, robots arrive, so I have time to get good at something.
I'd still be at Greenhill or on a **small place** with Sam.
The **yearly grant** worries me more than robots.
do: Do the **part-time agriculture certificate** over two years.
Use **AI for planning** as it improves.

S4.quote: Ten years makes dreams feel less silly.
fieldNote: With a decade, her focus shifts to **running a farm**, not just working on one.

A small place with **Sam** is a dream she's only half willing to say aloud.

steps.text: Study a part-time agriculture certificate over two years
Stay on as stock and veg worker at Greenhill
Keep saving a little each month for a future smallholding

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because places like Greenhill would be priced out before anyone had a plan. What would help is long-term funding for community farms, not one-year grants, and a basic income so people can keep doing work that matters even if it doesn't make money. And free college courses for farm workers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what farms are for. If farms are only for cheap food, then robots win. If farms are also for people, someone has to pay for that on purpose.

headlineQuote: If farms are only for cheap food, then robots win.
portrait: Freya is a **27-year-old** stock and veg worker at **Greenhill Community Farm**, run by a land trust.
Her wage depends partly on a **yearly council grant**, which worries her more than AI.
She lives with **Sam**, a nurse, whose steady income feels like both comfort and pressure.
She uses AI **now and then** and adopts tools after a season of proof.
Only **AGI by 2028** makes her anxious; with more time she'd **retrain** and stay hopeful.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because community farms like Greenhill would be priced out **first**.
whatWouldHelp: **Long-term funding** for community farms and a **basic income**.
